chapter: Hite tours, postwar L.A. and the Central Avenue scene
title: Leaving Hampton: Jack McVea and rhythm-and-blues sessions
summary: After 1942 he mostly recorded blues backing for Jack McVea and others.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: It says you left the band in '42 to
play lengthy engagements with Jack MacVeigh and Eddie Haywood and then to settle in Southern California.

There was no lengthy engagements. The engagements -- most of my time, when I worked with Jack MacVeigh, it was strictly recording jobs because he had an in with one of the rhythm and blues companies, which later -- I don't know if at that time it was called Cadette (PHONETIC) Records. That's what it was later called, with the Baharry (PHONETIC) Brothers. Jules Baharry and some -- and --
Michael, was that the other name?
I don't know. So, practically every week we would be recording with somebody with background for some blues singer. Half the time, you wouldn't know what his name was and sometimes you would.
This was here in Los Angeles?
Right here. People like Little Miss Cornshucks and Winonie Harris (PHONETIC), those sort of things.
